pos: n. pl. (the watermelons of Egypt; one of the five foods Israel named in the wilderness when they wearied of manna)
etymology: Greek melopepon, an apple-gourd, through Latin. The Hebrew abattichim is the watermelon of the Nile valley, a fruit of great abundance and cheapness in Egypt.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in a complaint: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). Five vegetables and a fish, named with the exactness of men who have been thinking about them. The next verse gives the contrast they meant to draw: “But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes” (Num 11:6). Nothing at all, beside this manna — bread from heaven, gathered fresh every morning, called nothing. The word freely in verse five is the tell: they had eaten these things at no cost, they said, in a land where their lives were made bitter with hard bondage. Memory had edited the price out. Exodus records the same trick earlier: “when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full” (Exo 16:3), said by men who had been slaves. A melon is not a sin. Preferring the melons of the house of bondage to the bread of God is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the melon as a plant and its fruit, of the cucumber kind, cultivated in warm climates for its large succulent fruit.
webster_full: MELON, n. [L. melo.] The name of certain plants and their fruit, as the muskmelon and the watermelon.
The watermelon is cultivated in warm climates, and its fruit is large and juicy.
The cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks. Num. xi.
MELON-THISTLE, n. A plant of the genus Cactus.
scriptures: Num 11:5
We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
Exo 16:3

And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.
corruption_summary: Nostalgia is trusted as memory, though Numbers 11 preserves a remembered Egypt in which slavery has been deleted and the vegetables are free.
corruption_paragraphs: The list in Numbers 11:5 is one of the most psychologically exact sentences in the Old Testament. Men who had been beaten in brickyards recall the produce market. They remember the fish; they specify five vegetables; and they insert one word that gives the whole account away — freely. Nothing was free in Egypt. The price of those melons was a whole people's children in the river and their lives made bitter with hard bondage. What the passage exposes is not a lie told to others but a memory that has quietly reorganised itself around a present dissatisfaction. That is how nostalgia works in every age: the difficulty of the present is real, so the past is edited until it can serve as an indictment of God's current dealing.

The second half of the complaint is the graver one. There is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes. They were being fed daily by a miracle so constant that it had become invisible, and the word for it was nothing. Familiarity does that to mercy. The Christian equivalent needs no elaboration: an open Bible, a preached gospel, a Lord's Day, a table, a household that eats every day — and the settled feeling that there is nothing at all before our eyes. Exodus 16:31 records what manna actually tasted like: wafers made with honey. The problem was never the flavour. Israel wanted a food that came from somewhere they could see, and a life that did not require them to gather it fresh each morning at God's hand.

pos: n. (a pungent bulb of the onion kind; last named in Israel's list of what Egypt gave them)
etymology: Old English garleac, from gar, a spear, and leac, a leek — the spear-leek, named for its pointed leaves. The Hebrew shum occurs only in Numbers 11:5.
biblical_def: It stands at the end of the list: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). Garlic was a staple of the Egyptian labourer — strong, cheap, and eaten with bread — and its appearing last gives the sentence its rhythm and its pathos. This is what the exodus was weighed against. The setting is a whole camp weeping in the doors of their tents, the mixt multitude falling a lusting and the children of Israel weeping with them, and the anger of the LORD kindled greatly; and the same chapter shows Moses at the end of himself, asking whether he had conceived all this people. Quails came, and with them a plague, and the place was named the graves of lust. Nothing in Scripture forbids garlic. What Numbers 11 records is an appetite that had grown loud enough to speak for the whole congregation, and a God who granted the request and sent leanness with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines garlic as a plant of the genus Allium, having a bulbous root of a strong and offensive smell and a pungent taste, much used in cookery.
webster_full: GARLIC, n. [Sax. garleac; gar, a dart, and leac, a leek.] A plant of the genus Allium.
The root is bulbous, of a strong and offensive smell, and an acrid pungent taste.
The leeks, and the onions, and the garlick. Num. xi.
GARLIC-EATER, n. A low fellow. [Not used.]
scriptures: Num 11:5
We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
corruption_summary: Appetite is treated as a fixed given to be satisfied rather than a servant to be governed, and Numbers 11 shows a whole nation moved by it.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's phrase for a certain kind of man is blunt: whose God is their belly. He is writing about professing enemies of the cross, and the mark he gives is not gross debauchery but a life organised around appetite. Numbers 11 shows a nation in that condition for a season. They are not worshipping an idol; they are naming vegetables, and weeping. The camp's grievance is genuinely felt, widely shared, and completely unanswerable by argument, which is what makes appetite so powerful in a community: it does not have to make a case. Modern life is arranged to keep every appetite within a few minutes' reach and to present the satisfying of them as a duty to oneself, so that the very idea of denying an appetite reads as self-harm rather than as discipline. The fasting the church has almost entirely lost was the ordinary Christian answer.

The chapter's outcome deserves to be preached whole. God gave them what they asked. Quails came in from the sea, and they had flesh a whole month, and while it was yet between their teeth the wrath of God fell, and the place was named Kibrothhattaavah — the graves of lust. The psalmist summarises it in a line that ought to make any man careful what he insists on: he gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul. That is a real and terrible mercy withheld: not every denied prayer is a hard providence, and not every granted one is a kindness. Proverbs sets the whole matter at a table, where it belongs: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.

“Whose God is their belly” — the New Testament's blunt name for the condition.
“Better is a dinner of herbs where love is” — the same table, weighed differently.

pos: n. pl. (a plant of the onion kind; third in Israel's list of Egyptian food)
etymology: Old English leac, a plant of the onion family — the same element in garlick and in hemlock. The Hebrew chatsir ordinarily means grass or green herbage, and is rendered leeks only here.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the same verse as the melons and the garlick: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). The Hebrew behind it is worth noticing, because chatsir is the word used for the grass that withereth and for the green thing that springs up — the commonest, cheapest growth there is. Israel is grieving over greens. That is exactly the force the passage wants: the things they wept for were not delicacies but the ordinary fare of a labouring people, and they still weighed more in the moment than manna and a promised land. Moses' own words in the chapter show what the complaint cost the man who had to carry it — he asks whether he begat this people, and whether he is to carry them in his bosom as a nursing father. The leeks of Egypt broke a prophet before they were done.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the leek as a plant of the genus Allium, cultivated for its bulb and leaves, allied to the onion and garlic.
webster_full: LEEK, n. [Sax. leac.] A plant of the genus Allium, having a bulbous root and long green leaves.
It is cultivated for kitchen use, and is allied to the onion.
The leeks, and the onions, and the garlick. Num. xi.
LEEK-GREEN, a. Of a green color resembling that of a leek.

We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
Num 11:6

Exo 16:3

And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith.
corruption_summary: Complaint is now spoken of as honesty and even as courage, while Scripture calls the murmuring of Numbers 11 what it was and records what it cost.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between lament and murmuring, which Scripture draws sharply and our vocabulary has lost. Lament is addressed to God, argues with Him on the basis of His own promises, and is all through the Psalms; a third of the Psalter is complaint, and God put it in the songbook. Murmuring is spoken about God to one another, it re-narrates the past to indict Him, and it spreads. Numbers 11 is murmuring: the people wept in the doors of their tents, every man in the door of his tent, and the complaint moved outward through the camp until Moses himself was undone by it. The test is not whether a man is sad or even angry — Job was both — but whether he is taking it to God or circulating it.

The second thing worth marking is what murmuring does to leadership. Moses' response in this chapter is one of the frankest speeches in the Old Testament: he tells God the burden is too heavy, that he did not conceive this people, and that if this is how it is to be he would rather be killed out of hand. God does not rebuke him. He appoints seventy elders and puts of the spirit upon them, dividing the load. That is providence answering exhaustion with help rather than with a reprimand, and it is worth remembering by anyone carrying a congregation, a household, or a company of murmurers. The leeks were the smallest thing imaginable to break a man over. They still nearly did.

pos: n. pl. (a trailing garden vegetable; named in Egypt's list, and giving Isaiah his picture of ruined Zion)
etymology: Latin cucumis. The Hebrew qishshuim is the Egyptian cucumber or gherkin, grown in irrigated plots along the Nile and, in Isaiah, in the walled gardens of Judah.
biblical_def: The word appears in two very different places. In the wilderness complaint it heads the list: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). In Isaiah it supplies one of the loneliest images in the prophets: “And the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a besieged city” (Isa 1:8). A lodge in a cucumber garden was a rough shelter thrown up for a watchman during the season and abandoned when the crop was in — a stick frame standing alone in an empty field, going to pieces in the weather. That is Jerusalem after the invasions: not destroyed, which would be simpler, but left. And then the verse that follows, which is the whole gospel of the chapter: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah” (Isa 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the cucumber as a plant of the genus Cucumis, and its fruit, much cultivated in gardens and used at the table.
webster_full: CUCUMBER, n. [L. cucumis.] An annual plant of the genus Cucumis, and its fruit.
The stems are trailing and armed with tendrils; the fruit is oblong and eaten raw or pickled.
As a lodge in a garden of cucumbers. Isa. i.
CUCURBITE, n. A chemical vessel in the shape of a gourd.

And the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a besieged city.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Num 11:5
We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
corruption_summary: A remnant is treated as a failure of the promise, though Isaiah 1:9 makes the remnant the only reason there was anyone left to complain of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the remnant runs from Noah to the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal to the election of grace in Romans 11, and it is regularly heard as a disappointment: God meant to save a nation and got a fragment. Isaiah 1:9 says the opposite. Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom. The remnant is not what is left over after failure; it is what God preserved against a judgment that would otherwise have been total. Paul quotes this exact verse in Romans 9 to prove the same point about Israel in his own day, and adds in the next chapter that at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. Small numbers are not evidence that God has lost; they are frequently the evidence that He has preserved.

The picture Isaiah uses says something further about how a church or a nation is left. The lodge in a cucumber garden was not destroyed. It was built for a season, used, and then abandoned when the crop came in — and it stands in the empty field looking exactly like what it is: a structure nobody needs any more. Institutional Christianity in a declining nation has that shape, and the passage is honest about how it happens. Isaiah's first chapter has already listed the cause: a people laden with iniquity, whose new moons and appointed feasts God's soul hateth, whose hands are full of blood, and whose remedy is stated in the plainest imperative in the book — wash you, make you clean, put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes.

pos: n. pl. (dried grapes in clusters; carried in Abigail's peace offering and given to a dying Egyptian in the field)
etymology: Old French raisin, a grape, from Latin racemus, a cluster. The Hebrew tsimmuqim means dried or shrivelled grapes, always counted in clusters and always part of a provision carried on the road.
biblical_def: Twice the word appears, and both scenes are about food given at the right moment. Abigail: “Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses” (1Sa 25:18). Her husband Nabal — a man the chapter calls churlish and evil in his doings (1Sa 25:3) — had refused David's men bread and water; his wife loaded a provision train, went down the covert of the hill, and stopped a massacre. David's answer is the verdict of heaven on her errand: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me” (1Sa 25:32). The other scene is in the Amalekite pursuit: David's men find a collapsed Egyptian slave in a field, give him bread and water (1Sa 30:11), and then “they gave him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins: and when he had eaten, his spirit came again to him: for he had eaten no bread, nor drunk any water, three days and three nights” (1Sa 30:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a raisin as a dried grape, cured either on the vine or by artificial heat, and used both as food and in medicine.
webster_full: RAISIN, n. s as z. [Fr. raisin, a grape; L. racemus.] A dried grape.
Grapes are suffered to remain on the vine till they are perfectly ripe, and then dried in the sun or by the heat of an oven.
An hundred clusters of raisins. 1 Sam. xxv.
Raisins are used in cookery and in medicine.
scriptures: Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses.

Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.

And they gave him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins: and when he had eaten, his spirit came again to him: for he had eaten no bread, nor drunk any water, three days and three nights.
And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me:
corruption_summary: Abigail is claimed for two opposite programmes — as a warrant for a wife to act against her husband, and as an embarrassment to be explained away — while the text commends her wisdom and never dissolves the marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is unusually careful about Abigail and it will not fund either party that uses her. She is called a woman of good understanding; her husband is called churlish and evil in his doings; she acts without telling him, and she prevents a slaughter. That is commended in the plainest terms by David, who blesses God for sending her and blesses her advice for keeping him from avenging himself with his own hand. So the passage does establish that a wife's submission is not a mandate to assist evil or to stand by while blood is shed, and Scripture never asks a wife to sin. What the passage does not do is dissolve the household or celebrate independence. Abigail returns home, finds Nabal drunk at a feast like a king, waits until morning, and tells him — and it is God, not she, who smites him ten days later. She acts to save life and then goes back to a marriage she did not leave.

The Egyptian in the field is a smaller story with a longer reach. He was a slave whose own master had abandoned him sick, three days without food or water, left to die in open country. David's men found him, fed him, gave him water, then figs and two clusters of raisins — and his spirit came again to him. Only afterwards does the account mention that he could lead them to the raiding party. The order is the point: bread first, and the intelligence follows as a gift rather than as the price. Where a ministry of mercy is undertaken only as a lever for something else, the Egyptian in this chapter is the standing rebuke; and where mercy is shown for its own sake, God has a way of adding what no strategy could have bought.

pos: n. pl. (a field pulse; part of the provision brought to David in the wilderness by three men when his own son had driven him out)
etymology: Old English bean. The Hebrew pol is the broad or horse bean, a staple of the poor, listed among the ingredients of Ezekiel's siege bread as well as in David's relief train.
biblical_def: The word occurs in one of the most moving supply lists in Scripture. David has fled Jerusalem before Absalom, crossed Jordan and come to Mahanaim, and three men meet him there — Shobi an Ammonite, Machir of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite (2Sa 17:27). They “brought beds, and basons, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse” (2Sa 17:28), and then the rest: “And honey, and butter, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness” (2Sa 17:29). The reason given is one plain sentence with no theology in it at all. Note who brought it. Shobi was of Ammon, whose city David had taken; Machir of Lodebar had once sheltered Mephibosheth, Saul's crippled grandson. Men with every reason to stay clear brought beds and beans to a king with nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the bean as a plant and its seed, of the genus Vicia and related kinds, cultivated for food for man and beast.
webster_full: BEAN, n. [Sax. bean.] A name given to several kinds of pulse, or leguminous seeds, and the plants producing them.
The horse-bean is cultivated for cattle; the garden beans for the table.
Wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans. 2 Sam. xvii.
BEAN-CAPER, n. A plant, a species of Zygophyllum.
scriptures: Brought beds, and basons, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse,
And honey, and butter, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness.
And it came to pass, when David was come to Mahanaim, that Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim,
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
corruption_summary: Practical help is spoken of as a lesser form of ministry than teaching or advice, though Scripture records the beds and the beans by name and gives the reason in one sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary provision. When David's kingdom collapsed and his own son hunted him, the help that arrived was not counsel and not a prophecy; it was beds, basons, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentiles, pulse, honey, butter, sheep and cheese. The Holy Ghost saw fit to list every item. And the stated reason is as plain as the list: the people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness. James says the same thing negatively — if a brother or sister be naked and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled, notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body, what doth it profit?

The three men are worth naming, because each had a reason not to come. Shobi was son of Nahash of Rabbah, of the children of Ammon — a house David had warred against. Machir of Lodebar was the man who had kept Mephibosheth, Saul's lame grandson, before David sent for him. Barzillai was a very great man of Gilead, eighty years old, who would later decline the king's offer of a place at court and ask only to die in his own city. Old enemies, old loyalties to a rival house, and a rich man with nothing to gain: these are who showed up at Mahanaim with beans. Providence supplies a fugitive king through the men one would least predict, and it does so through means so ordinary that a reader in a hurry passes the verse without noticing that it is the answer to a prayer.

“The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty” — the whole reason given.
Shobi, Machir and Barzillai — the three least likely men in Israel.

pos: n. (curdled milk pressed into a mass; brought to David in exile, and used by Job as a figure of his own forming in the womb)
etymology: Old English cyse, from Latin caseus. The Hebrew at 2 Samuel 17 is shephoth baqar, cheese of kine; at Job 10 the verb qapha means to curdle or congeal.
biblical_def: Cheese appears in the relief train at Mahanaim: “And honey, and butter, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness” (2Sa 17:29). Then Job uses cheese-making for something far greater: “Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?” (Job 10:10), and the next verse continues the figure: “Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11). Job is arguing with God in the middle of his affliction and his argument is that God made him — poured him out, curdled him, clothed him, fenced him — and therefore knows exactly what He is dealing with. It is one of the earliest and most vivid statements in Scripture of the forming of a child in the womb by the direct workmanship of God, and it is used not as an abstract doctrine but as a plea. David says the same in a different key: “I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psa 139:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cheese as the curd of milk, coagulated by rennet, separated from the whey and pressed into a mass in a hoop or vat.
webster_full: CHEESE, n. [Sax. cyse; L. caseus.] The curd or thick part of milk, coagulated and pressed into a mass.
Cheese of kine. 2 Sam. xvii.
CHEESE-PRESS, n. A press or engine for pressing curd in the making of cheese.
CHEESE-VAT, n. The vat or case in which curds are confined for pressing.
scriptures: And honey, and butter, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness.
Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?
Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews.
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: The unborn child is spoken of as a process rather than a person, while Job and David both address God directly as the maker of what they were before they were born.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 10:10-11 and Psalm 139:13-16 are the two great passages on the forming of a child, and they share a grammar that settles the question. Both are addressed to God in the second person about the speaker in the first person. Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh. Not it, and not the tissue that became me: me. The continuity of the person from the earliest stage is assumed in the very structure of the sentence, and neither writer is making an argument about it — Job is pleading and David is praising, which is stronger evidence than an argument, because it shows what they took for granted. The modern habit of describing the unborn as a process, a potential, or a cluster of developing tissue is not a scientific refinement of these verses; it is a different account of who is there.

It is worth noticing what Job does with the doctrine, because it is not what a comfortable reader expects. He is not consoling himself. He is arguing: thou hast made me, and dost thou destroy me? remember that thou hast made me as the clay. The doctrine of God's workmanship in the womb is here the ground of a complaint brought to God's own face, and God does not rebuke Job for bringing it. That gives a suffering believer more room than most preaching allows him. A Christian may say to God, in the middle of an affliction he does not understand, that God Himself poured him out and curdled him and fenced him with bones, and ask what He is doing. Job ends the book with his hand on his mouth, but he does not get there by being forbidden to speak.
roots_summary: Hebrew shephoth (H8194), cheeses, at 2 Samuel 17:29; gebinah (H1385), cheese, at Job 10:10; with qapha (H7087), to curdle or congeal.
roots_lines: Hebrew shephoth baqar — cheese of kine; part of the provision at Mahanaim; 2 Samuel 17:29.
Hebrew gebinah (H1385) — cheese; curdled me like cheese; Job 10:10.
Hebrew qapha (H7087) — to curdle, to congeal, to thicken; the verb of the forming; Job 10:10.
Hebrew sakak (H5526) — to cover, to fence in; thou hast fenced me with bones and sinews; Job 10:11.
Hebrew raqam (H7551) — to embroider; curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth; Psalm 139:15.
usage: “Cheese of kine, for David, and for the people” — ordinary food in a hard place.
“Curdled me like cheese” — a kitchen figure for the making of a man.
“I am fearfully and wonderfully made” — the same doctrine, sung instead of pleaded.

pos: n. (a seed of the parsley kind; twice used to describe the appearance of the manna)
etymology: Greek koriannon, through Latin coriandrum. The Hebrew gad names the same small round seed, familiar in every Near Eastern kitchen and therefore the natural comparison for something no one had seen before.
biblical_def: Both uses describe the manna, and between them they give its look, its colour and its taste. “And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey” (Exo 16:31). Numbers adds the further comparison to bdellium (Num 11:7). The choice of coriander is itself instructive: to describe an unprecedented thing, Scripture reaches for the most ordinary object in a household. The name the people gave it works the same way — manna, from their first question, what is it?, so that Israel ate a food whose name was a question for forty years. And it fell six mornings a week, doubled on the sixth, bred worms if hoarded, and stopped the day after they ate the old corn of the land. The Lord Jesus took up the whole account and settled its meaning: your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead; I am that bread of life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coriander as an annual plant, the seeds of which have a strong smell and are used in medicine and confectionery.
webster_full: CORIANDER, n. [L. coriandrum.] A plant, the Coriandrum sativum.
The seeds are round, of an agreeable smell when dried, and used in cookery and medicine.
It was like coriander seed, white. Ex. xvi.
The green herb has a strong disagreeable scent.
scriptures: And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.
Exo 16:3

And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
Num 11:5
We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
corruption_summary: The manna is explained away as a natural secretion of the tamarisk, and the explanation cannot account for a single one of the details Scripture actually gives.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard naturalistic account identifies manna with the sweet excretion left on tamarisk twigs by scale insects in the Sinai. It is a real substance, and it explains nothing in Exodus 16. That manna fell six days and not the seventh; that a double portion fell on the sixth day; that what was kept overnight bred worms and stank, while the sabbath portion kept sweet; that every man gathered according to his eating and, when measured, he that gathered much had nothing over and he that gathered little had no lack; that it fed some two million people for forty years across changing terrain; and that it ceased the day after they ate of the old corn of the land of Canaan. No insect keeps a sabbath. The account is either a miracle or an invention, and the tamarisk is not a middle way.

What the coriander comparison guards against is the opposite error, which is to make the miracle so exotic that it stops being food. The manna is described in the plainest kitchen terms available — the size and shape of a coriander seed, white, tasting like a honey wafer — and it had to be gathered, ground, beaten and baked. God's supernatural provision came in a form a woman could cook. That is the shape of nearly all His giving: an ordinary loaf multiplied, water made wine at a village wedding, a Saviour born in a stable and called a carpenter's son. The Lord Jesus made the manna the text of the great discourse at Capernaum, and the offence there was exactly its ordinariness — is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?
roots_summary: Hebrew gad (H1407), coriander seed; with man (H4478), manna, from man hu, what is it; and tsappichith (H6838), a honey wafer.
roots_lines: Hebrew gad (H1407) — coriander; it was like coriander seed, white; Exodus 16:31, Numbers 11:7.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; named from the people's question, what is it; Exodus 16:15.
Hebrew tsappichith (H6838) — a flat cake or wafer; the taste of it was like wafers made with honey; Exodus 16:31.
Hebrew bedolach (H916) — bdellium; the colour comparison added in Numbers; Numbers 11:7.
Greek artos tes zoes — the bread of life; the Lord's own interpretation of the manna; John 6:35.
usage: “Like coriander seed, white” — an unprecedented thing described by a kitchen staple.
“The taste of it was like wafers made with honey” — and they called it nothing at all.
“What is it?” — a food whose name stayed a question for forty years.

pos: n. (the chief meal; in the Gospels the occasion of a parable, a rebuke about washing, and a rule about the guest list)
etymology: Old French disner, to dine, from a Latin root meaning to break the fast. The Greek ariston is the earlier meal of the day, distinguished from deipnon, the supper.
biblical_def: Scripture puts a remarkable amount of teaching at a table. Proverbs: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith” (Pro 15:17) — the menu is not the meal. The parable of the marriage: “Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage” (Mat 22:4), and the refusal is not hostility but indifference — “they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise” (Mat 22:5). A Pharisee's table: “And when the Pharisee saw it, he marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner” (Luk 11:38), which opens the woes on ceremonial cleanness without inward cleanness. And the guest list: “When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee” (Luk 14:12); instead, “call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dinner as the meal taken about the middle of the day, or the principal meal of the day; also an entertainment, a feast.
webster_full: DINNER, n. [Fr. diner.] The meal taken about the middle of the day; or the principal meal of the day, eaten between noon and evening.
2. An entertainment; a feast.
Behold, I have prepared my dinner. Matt. xxii.
DINNER-TIME, n. The time of dining.
scriptures: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Mat 22:4
Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage.

Then said he also to him that bade him, When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee.
But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:
corruption_summary: Hospitality has become entertaining — a display for those who can return it — which is precisely the arrangement Luke 14:12 forbids by name.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's instruction at that table is one of the least obeyed sentences in the Gospels, and its logic is exact. Call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours — and the reason given is not that such people are bad company but that they will bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee. A dinner that will be repaid is a transaction, and it has already been paid for. Call instead the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind, who cannot recompense thee, and thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just. What our own culture calls hospitality is very largely entertaining: a room prepared, a standard maintained, an audience able to reciprocate, and considerable anxiety about the presentation. Biblical hospitality is a table set for people who cannot return it, and Hebrews adds that some have entertained angels unawares.

The parable of the marriage dinner adds the other half. The king's invitation is refused not by enemies but by the invited, who made light of it and went their ways — one to his farm, another to his merchandise. Neither errand is sinful; a farm and a business are lawful things, and that is what makes the refusal so ordinary and so damning. The gospel is not usually rejected by argument. It is crowded out by legitimate occupations from men who fully intend to attend some other time. And when the bidden would not come, the servants were sent into the highways to gather all they found, both bad and good, and the wedding was furnished with guests — which is a picture of the Gentiles, and of every congregation of people who had no claim on the table they are eating at.
roots_summary: Greek ariston (G712), the earlier or chief meal, rendered dinner; with deipnon (G1173), supper, and antapodoma (G468), a recompence.
roots_lines: Greek ariston (G712) — a morning or midday meal, a dinner; I have prepared my dinner; Matthew 22:4, Luke 14:12.
Greek deipnon (G1173) — the evening meal, a supper, a banquet; the marriage supper of the Lamb; Revelation 19:9.
Greek antapodoma (G468) — a recompence, a return payment; lest a recompence be made thee; Luke 14:12.
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; be not forgetful to entertain strangers; Hebrews 13:2.
Hebrew aruchah (H737) — an allowance of food, a meal; better is a dinner of herbs where love is; Proverbs 15:17.
usage: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is” — the menu is not the meal.
“They made light of it, and went their ways” — the refusal that is not hostility.
“Call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” — guests who cannot bid thee again.

pos: n. (a liquid; in the law the juice of grapes forbidden to the Nazarite, not a distilled spirit)
etymology: Latin liquor, a fluid, from liquere, to be liquid. In 1611 English the word means simply a liquid or a juice; the modern restriction to distilled spirits is later and misleads a hasty reader of the Nazarite law.
biblical_def: The Nazarite's separation is described by a widening series of prohibitions: “He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried” (Num 6:3). The law does not stop at intoxication. It moves outward from wine to vinegar, from vinegar to grape juice, from juice to fresh grapes, and from fresh grapes to raisins — and the following verse adds the kernels and the husk. The point is not that grapes are unclean; it is that a man under a vow of separation abstains from the whole field of a lawful thing for the term of his vow, as a visible sign. The other use is in the Song: “Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor” (Son 7:2). Amos names the sin of a generation that would not let separated men keep their vow: “But ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink; and commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not” (Amo 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liquor as a liquid or fluid substance; and specifically, spirituous fluids — noting the general sense first, as any liquid or juice.
webster_full: LIQUOR, n. lik'or. [L. liquor.] A liquid or fluid substance.
Liquor is a word of general signification, extending to water, milk, blood, sap, juice, &c.
2. Spirituous fluids; a sense in which the word is most frequently used.
Neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes. Num. vi.
scriptures: Num 6:3
He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried.
Jdg 13:5

For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.
Amo 2:12
But ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink; and commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not.
Son 7:2
Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.
corruption_summary: The Nazarite vow is enlisted on both sides of the drink question, though the law binds only the separated man for the term of his vow and the same law commands wine as a drink offering.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 6 is quoted as though it were the Bible's general standard for drink, and it is not. It is a voluntary vow, for a stated term, binding those who take it, and its severity is the whole point: even the raisins are forbidden, and a man is not more holy for keeping the vow than a man who never took it. The same Pentateuch commands a drink offering of wine with the daily sacrifice, allows the tithe to be spent on wine or strong drink in a feast before the LORD, and Psalm 104 says God gives wine that maketh glad the heart of man. The New Testament never revokes this; the Lord made wine at Cana, instituted a Supper with the fruit of the vine, and Paul told Timothy to take a little for his stomach's sake. What Scripture forbids without qualification is drunkenness, which it names as a work of the flesh that shuts men out of the kingdom.

The abuse in the other direction is Amos's, and it is the more revealing. God's complaint against Israel is not that Nazarites drank but that ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink — a nation deliberately breaking down other men's consecration, in the same breath as it told the prophets to stop prophesying. Those two sins belong together. A generation that will not hear preaching cannot bear the sight of visible separation either, because both are a standing rebuke. The application is not far off. Where a Christian abstains, fasts, keeps a sabbath, or orders his household by a rule that costs him something, there is a persistent social pressure to get him to break it — usually offered as kindness. Amos calls that pressure a transgression, and lists it with commanding the prophets to be silent.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishrah (H4952), juice or infusion of grapes; with nazir (H5139), a separated one, and nazar (H5144), to separate oneself by vow.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishrah (H4952) — juice, liquor of grapes; forbidden to the Nazarite; Numbers 6:3.
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, a Nazarite; the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb; Judges 13:5.
Hebrew shekar (H7941) — strong drink; distinguished from wine throughout the law; Numbers 6:3.
Hebrew shemer — lees, the dregs of wine; the figure of settled men in Zephaniah 1:12.
Greek methe (G3178) — drunkenness; named as a work of the flesh; Galatians 5:21.
usage: “Neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes” — and no raisins either, for the term of a vow.
“A Nazarite unto God from the womb” — a separation appointed before birth.
“Ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink” — naming the breaking of another man's vow as sin.
